Recent work supports text-derived item representations for sparse-item recommendation, but the retrieved 2023–2026 papers do not establish a directly matching, from-scratch GRU4Rec solution. [TASTE (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.14029) reports improved long-tail recommendations and reduced popularity bias through textual matching, but uses pretrained language models. [CALRec (2024)](https://research.google/pubs/calrec-contrastive-alignment-of-generative-llms-for-sequential-recommendation/) aligns user histories and item descriptions through contrastive objectives, also relying on a pretrained LLM. These provide motivation rather than eligible architectures under the stated constraints.

The closest foundational precedent is [Ask the GRU (2016)](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.02116): jointly learns a GRU text encoder with collaborative recommendation, demonstrating cold-start benefits; also finds supervised mean-pooled word embeddings competitive. Its user model is matrix factorization, so it does not directly validate a sequential GRU backbone. A constraint-compatible hypothesis is to learn randomly initialized token embeddings over titles/descriptions, pool them with a small projection or text GRU, and combine that vector with the item-ID embedding inside one jointly trained GRU4Rec network. Share this item representation between history inputs and candidate scoring, using one recommendation score and checkpoint per category. This adaptation requires validation; cited gains do not establish improvements on the pinned benchmark. Exclude the paper’s tag/genre auxiliary objectives because those attributes are unavailable.
